## Why Ding-Chou can be auspicious or ominous, and the hand-seal sequence


Today, a Ding-Chou day, is one of the seven great White Tiger days (백호살) among the sixty cycle days. Its energy is condensed to the extreme. Maybe that's why the market is in such chaos.

In Body-Qimen, the Jade Maiden (옥녀 玉女) carries the energy of Ding-fire. She gently melts the Geng-metal energy that attacks Jia-wood (갑목 甲木).

So depending on the earthly branch it meets, Ding-fire can create an auspicious formation (길격 吉格), or an ominous one (흉격 凶格) in which nothing works.

The mechanism in one sentence: "When Ding-fire (丁火), the moving starlight, enters a particular direction (branch) of the nine palaces, it meets the heavenly stem already lying at the bottom of that direction, the hidden stem (지장간 地藏干), and automatically sparks an auspicious formation (a chemical spark)."

Everything depends on the bond Ding forms with the palace's owner (its stem) at the moment it settles into that palace (branch).

In Body-Qimen this is done with hand seals (수인 手印):

- **Left hand holds Former-Heaven Li ☲** = switch on the heavenly Ding-fire (丁火 · Jade Maiden).
- **Right hand holds one of the six Later-Heaven palaces** (Zhen, Xun, Kun, Dui, Qian, Gen) = call up the hidden stem concealed in that palace's branch (Mao, Si, Wei, You, Hai, Chou).
- **The two hands interlock** = Ding plus the hidden stem combine, and Qimen Dunjia's six great auspicious formations activate inside your own body.

**Why is it sometimes auspicious and sometimes ominous?**

Looking only at the stems, Ding + Xin (丁+辛), Ding + Gui (丁+癸), or Ding-fire entering the Gen palace (Chou-earth), which is called "striking punishment" (격형 擊刑), are classed in space-time Qimen Dunjia as difficult or ominous.

Ding-Chou is the image of Ding-fire, the starlight and candle flame of heaven, set on top of Chou-earth, the frozen winter mud of the ground and the storehouse of metal.

You *can* use the Ding-Chou Jade Maiden as a great auspicious formation: "lighting a lamp to open a dark treasure vault." But if your body's condition (its fire timing, 화후 火候) or the order in which you use the energies is off, Ding-Chou turns into one of the hardest ominous formations in Qimen, destiny reading (명리), and neidan alike.

**1) Fire generates earth, but not every earth welcomes fire.**

- *The nature of Chou-earth:* the Chou month, which holds Minor Cold and Great Cold, is the coldest, darkest stretch of deep winter: frozen, waterlogged mud (습토 濕土).
- *The flame suffocates (회화 晦火):* if the basic yang-qi of the lower belly (lower dantian; Qian-metal ☰) has not been warmed up at all, and you rashly take only the Ding-Chou seal (left Li ☲ + right Gen ☶), the little candle (Ding-fire) is crushed by the damp of the cold mud. It loses its light, smokes, and goes out.
- *Ding-fire enters the tomb (입묘 入墓):* by the twelve life stages, Chou is Ding-fire's tomb (묘지 墓地), where its energy goes into the grave. Go in unprepared and instead of opening the vault, the starlight of your own awareness (the Jade Maiden) gets trapped in a cold tomb. You fall into lethargy, low mood, or deep exhaustion (a drained battery).

**2) Open the belly of the character Chou (its hidden stems)** and three things lie coiled there: Gui-water (癸水, cold rain), Xin-metal (辛金, a sharp gem or needle), and Ji-earth (己土, cloud or damp soil).

If Ding enters Chou with no protective shield, two Qimen ominous formations go off inside the hidden stems at once:

1. **Inner "Red Bird plunges into the river" (주작투강 朱雀投江, Ding + Gui):** the cold Gui-water hidden in Chou-earth rises and smothers Ding-fire's spark (water overcomes fire). In neidan practice this is when cold water (한수 寒水) in the lower belly puts out the faint warmth at the solar plexus. The belly goes cold, with diarrhea or indigestion.
2. **Inner "fire and metal at war" (화금상전 火金相戰, Ding + Xin):** if Ding touches the Xin-metal inside Chou-earth with weak, clumsy fire, it does not refine the gem. It only coats it in soot, and they clash in sparks (fire overcoming metal, backfiring). Qimen reads this as an ominous formation of getting tangled in disputes with a criminal (Xin-metal).

Ding-Chou is one of the seven great White Tiger days, its energy condensed to the extreme. When this high-pressure energy is well gathered in through neidan, it becomes explosive drive and the power to open the treasury (재물 개고 開庫). When control is lost, it shows up as side effects of qi and blood flowing backward in the body: rising blood pressure, sudden anger, muscle cramps, or nerve pain.

In the end, Ding-Chou turns ominous for one reason only: "you shoved a bare little candle (Ding-fire) into a cold, murky storehouse (Chou-earth)."

That is exactly why, when I gave today's Ding-Chou seal sequence earlier, I stressed that you must not go straight to *Bi* (山火賁 ䷕: Ding-Chou). You must first lay down *Great Taming* (山天大畜 ䷙) and then draw it out afterward with *Xian* (澤山咸 ䷞)!

- **Feeding in the Jade Maiden (refining the vault):** *Bi* ䷕, right hand Gen ☶ / left hand Li ☲. With the lower belly warm, lift only the left middle finger to switch on Ding-fire (Li ☲). Only the vault inside Chou-earth opens, safely, and the great auspicious formation "Jade Maiden in hidden treasure · opening the Chou-Wei storehouse" (옥녀암장 · 축미개고) starts working.

The legend of Za Rahula, tamed by Padmasambhava

Rahula (Za Rahula) is not an object of popular devotion that ordinary Buddhists worship to pray for blessings. His nature carries an extremely dangerous and fierce energy that strikes the nervous system and causes eclipses.

Instead, he has been strictly honored as a "supreme protector" (Dharmapala) who guards the purity of the teaching and smashes practitioners' demonic obstacles in Nyingma, the oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism, and in its highest practice system, Dzogchen (the Great Perfection).

A very tragic and intense Tibetan local legend lies behind how the Indian Rahu, coming into Tibetan tantra, was transformed into the terrible, fierce wrathful deity "Za Rahula" seen in the image earlier.

In ancient Tibet (or northern India) there was a great yogi who devoted himself only to practice deep in the mountains. He was deeply respected by the queen (or a patron) of a kingdom and received offerings from her. But jealous courtiers falsely accused him to the king: "That practitioner is having an affair with the queen."

The enraged king, without investigating, seized the yogi, tortured him terribly, and burned him alive (or threw him into a pit of vipers). At the moment of death, the yogi, who had practiced purely his whole life, was seized by extreme rage at human folly and the injustice done to him.

"I will become the being who brings the most terrible calamities upon this foolish world!"

His fierce resentment combined with his amplified practice energy, and right after death he was reborn as "Za Rahula," a terrible demon king with nine heads, thousands of eyes, and a serpent's lower body. Carrying a bow and arrows, he flew through the sky shooting arrows that caused strokes, epilepsy, and terrible epidemics, and he became an object of terror who even blotted out the sun and moon.

When cosmic calamity broke out, the great teacher Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche), founder of Tibetan tantra, or Vajrapani, the incarnation of wrath, stepped in.

Padmasambhava did not destroy Rahula.

Instead, after subduing (조복) his vast energy of rage and karma with the power of the Dharma, he showed him the ultimate truth of the universe and awakened his original clear Buddha-nature.

Realizing that his rage came from dualistic illusion, Rahula knelt before Padmasambhava and vowed: "From now on I will use this mighty power not to destroy the Dharma but to crush the obstacles and enemies who obstruct the deepest teaching of tantra (Dzogchen)."

After that, Za Rahula became one of the three most powerful protectors of the Dzogchen tradition. The arrows he shoots are no longer calamities that sicken the innocent, but a weapon of compassion that pierces and kills exactly the "tangles of energy" and the life of the "ego" that obstruct a practitioner's awakening.

Out of control, that powerful destructive force becomes stroke or paralysis (Rahula's arrows), but tuned by wisdom (Padmasambhava) it becomes the most powerful driving force to open the dimensional door of awakening. The essence of tantra is contained whole in this story.

Tögal: seeing with the heart for liberation, and the kati channel

[How to see with the heart for liberation]

Tögal means "leaping over the skull."

It isn't a road of piling up concepts, but a road on which the heart's luminosity bursts out through the eyes along a special energy pathway and directly shows its own nature in space.

If liberation is the goal, don't cling to this phenomenon as a mystery; let everything that appears go as the play of your own awareness.

The special pathway from the heart to the eyes is called the kati channel.

Kati is the passage through which that liberation bursts directly from the heart through the eyes. It's a different layer altogether from the ordinary tantric nadis (left, right, central channels).

It's a channel of luminosity that comes fully to light only in Dzogchen, especially in Tögal.

Starting from the "lamp of the flesh" (citta lamp of the flesh) in the very center of the heart, two strands transparent like hollow crystal tubes, about one-eighth the thickness of a horsehair, branch like the horns of a wild yak, go around behind the ears, and end at the pupils of both eyes.

See with the heart.

Mystifying this channel as a "special energy passage" and hiding it, or veiling it as "only for the qualified," is itself another attachment.

The real thing is to open your eyes, gaze into space, and directly confirm the moment the heart flows out through the eyes.

If you try to understand it as a concept, the brain blocks it again.

Just look.

From the heart, the eyes open.

The third eye as the ultimate cosmic eclipse

The third eye (ajna chakra) is not a cheap magic trick that opens out of nowhere on the forehead. It is the ultimate cosmic eclipse (일식 日食), produced when fundamental energy ignited in the deepest place of the heart, the indestructible drop, surges up the spine (central channel) and collides with the energy of the head.
